curriculum.reference: Essential Grammar in Use, Unit 4; owner outline; original teaching

title: Are you doing? — present continuous questions
learningObjective: Ask yes/no and information questions about ongoing actions and give natural short answers.
hook: You are working. Are you working? The action stays; be moves.
script:
In Unit 3, you are working describes an action now. Are you working asks about that same action. As in Unit 2, be moves before the subject. Working stays after the subject.

Look at the moving pen. The person is writing. Are you writing? We ask the person about this action. Yes, I am. The action is the same in the question and answer.

She is drawing becomes is she drawing? Move is before she. Keep drawing in its ing form. The question mark helps us read the question, but the word order must change too.

Start with am, is or are. Then the subject, then the ing action. Are they preparing lunch? The action phrase stays together. The same words can describe an action or ask about it.

With I, begin with am: am I speaking clearly? With he or she, begin with is. Is he listening? Is she reading? Keep the ing action in each question.

It still takes is: is it raining? You takes are: are you waiting? We keep the agreement from earlier units and put be first.

We and they also take are. Are we learning? Are they preparing lunch? Think of the subject first so you can choose the matching form of be.

The students is the whole subject here. Are the students preparing a presentation? Put are before the whole phrase. Do not put preparing between the and students.

You can see someone cooking. Is she cooking checks the action. What is she making asks you to name the food. Here she is making soup. What asks for information, not just yes or no.

You know question words from Unit 2. Start with what, then keep be before the subject: what are you drawing? What goes first because we want to know the thing being drawn.

Look at the shape on the paper: a roof, walls and a door. What are you drawing? A house. The reply names the thing, so what is the useful question word.

Watch the person move toward the library entrance. Where is he going? To the library. Where asks for a place. Your brother is a longer subject: where is your brother going?

Ava can hear her friends laughing. Why are they laughing? They are reading a funny story. Why asks for the reason for the action.

Ben is using his phone. Ava wants to know the person he is calling. Who are you calling? My dad. Who asks for a person. In this question, are still comes before you.

Ava checks on Ben after a rest. How are you feeling? I’m feeling better. How asks about his condition here. The answer gives information.

What are you looking at? A bird outside the window. Looking at tells us where someone directs their eyes. Keep at at the end here. The same question order still works: what, are, you, looking at.

Who are you talking to? My neighbour. Talking to connects the action with the other person. Keep to in this question. You do not need a new question pattern: who, are, you, talking to.

Ava asks Ben: are you cooking? Ben answers yes, I am. Ben calls himself I, so he uses am. He does not need to repeat cooking because Ava has already named the action.

Use the subject and be in a short yes answer. Yes, he is. Yes, she is. Yes, it is. Keep is at the end; the action is understood from the question.

The same short-answer pattern works with are. Yes, you are. Yes, we are. Yes, they are. Choose the subject for the person or people you mean.

Are you waiting for someone? No, I’m not. The answer means I am not waiting for someone. The short answer keeps the negative meaning without repeating the action.

With he, she or it, you can use isn’t. No, he isn’t. No, she isn’t. No, it isn’t. With you, we or they, use aren’t. The subject still chooses the form.

No, you aren’t. No, we aren’t. No, they aren’t. No, she’s not and no, we’re not are natural alternatives too. These patterns are familiar from Unit 2; the action is simply understood.

For a complete affirmative short answer, say yes, I am. Yes, I’m is not the normal complete answer on its own. No, she’s not and no, we’re not can use contractions because not remains.

Is she working checks whether the action is happening. Where is she working asks for a place: at the library. Listen to the beginning of the question to decide what kind of answer is needed.

What you are cooking leaves be after the subject. Move are before you: what are you cooking? What stays first and cooking stays after the subject.

Is working your sister puts the action before the subject. Say is your sister working? Your sister stays together. The order is is, the whole subject, then working.

Are the dog sleeping uses the wrong form of be. The dog is one animal, like it. Say is the dog sleeping? Keep sleeping. Only the be form needs correcting.

Ben is washing a cup. [Pause five seconds.] Is Ben washing a cup? Move is before Ben; keep washing after the subject.

Put in order: they / are / waiting [Pause five seconds.] Are they waiting? In a standard question, are comes before they.

___ I speaking too quietly? [Pause five seconds.] Am With I, use am before the subject.

___ your friends preparing lunch? [Pause five seconds.] Are Friends means they: use are.

Ask for a place: ___ is Ben going? [Pause five seconds.] Where Where asks for a place. Keep is before Ben.

Ask for a reason: ___ are they laughing? [Pause five seconds.] Why Why asks for the reason. Keep are before they.

Look at the person and the picture on the paper. In the next exercise, choose the question that checks this action. Keep the ing action and choose be for the subject.

Ava is drawing a house. Ask if she is drawing. [Pause five seconds.] Is Ava drawing? Put is before Ava. Keep drawing after Ava.

Ava asks you: Are you reading? Answer yes. [Pause five seconds.] Yes, I am. Use I for yourself. End with the full am.

Are the children sleeping? Answer no. [Pause five seconds.] No, they aren’t. The children means they. Use aren’t in the short no answer.

Who are you talking to? [Pause five seconds.] My neighbour. Who asks for a person, so name the person.

Put am, is or are before the subject. Keep the ing action. Add a question word when you want specific information. Use a natural short answer when the question asks for yes or no.

Are you making lunch? Yes, I am. What are you making? Soup. The first question checks the action; the second asks for information. Try asking someone near you about an action happening now.
